query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In body-centred-cubic refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) the dominant control on both high-temperature strength and thermo-elastic stiffness is the degree of chemical short-range order (SRO); increasing SRO (1–2 nm B2-like clusters rich in Nb-Ta vs Mo-W) raises the average bond stiffness, which (i) increases the elastic modulus and yield strength and (ii) lowers the coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE).
generation.material_initial_state: Arc-melted, homogenised, equiatomic Nb–Mo–Ta–W RHEA with grain size 10–30 µm, single-phase BCC solid solution, minimal prior cold work.
generation.intervention: Induce controllable SRO by low-temperature annealing (900 °C, 48 h, furnace-cooling) compared with a rapidly water-quenched specimen from 1600 °C that preserves a nearly random solid solution.
generation.conditions: Tests performed in vacuum/Ar from 25 °C to 1400 °C; strain rate 10-4 s-1 for compression tests; dilatometry heating rate 10 K min-1.
generation.structural_mediator: Volume fraction and correlation length of B2-like SRO clusters measured by neutron/x-ray diffuse scattering and atom-probe tomography.
generation.mechanism: SRO produces alternating strong/weak bond networks that (a) raise average force constants, giving a higher elastic modulus and lower vibrational entropy (reducing CTE), and (b) generate a spatially fluctuating Peierls potential that impedes screw-dislocation glide, raising high-temperature yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quenched, disorder-rich baseline, the SRO-enhanced alloy will show: • 8–12 % higher room-temperature Young’s modulus and ~5 % lower CTE. • ~20 % higher 0.2 % offset yield strength at 1000–1200 °C, with similar strain-rate sensitivity. • No significant change in grain size or texture, isolating SRO as the cause.
generation.baseline: Same alloy, identical processing up to homogenisation, but water-quenched from 1600 °C to suppress SRO (random solid solution).
generation.boundary: Effect expected only while single-phase BCC is stable (≈800–1500 °C) and for grain sizes >5 µm where GB strengthening is secondary. Deviates for heavily deformed, oxidised, or multiphase material.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of strength/modulus shifts could be smaller if SRO clusters coarsen or if quenched disorder is not fully retained; converse sign changes possible if different cluster chemistry forms.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two specimen sets as described (quenched vs annealed). Characterise SRO by neutron diffuse scattering (Huang scattering intensity vs Q) and 3-D atom-probe mapping. Measure (i) RT and high-T Young’s modulus by impulse excitation, (ii) 0.2 % yield strength in compression at 1000 °C and 1200 °C, (iii) CTE from 25–1200 °C with push-rod dilatometry.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (higher-SRO) specimens do NOT show (a) ≥5 % increase in modulus OR (b) ≥5 % decrease in CTE OR (c) ≥5 % increase in yield strength relative to quenched specimens, despite confirmed higher SRO, the hypothesis is falsified.
